questions.enonce_markdown:
This question concerns the d-block elements, Sulphur, Nitrogen and Group IV elements.

(a) (i) Distinguish between a d-block element and a transition metal.

(ii) Write down the symbols for the elements of the first transition series in increasing order of atomic number.

(iii) State the property of the transition element which enables them to act as catalyst in many industrial processes. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A **d-block element** is an element whose atoms have their outermost (highest-energy) electron in a **d sub-shell**, that is the elements of the block between group II and group III. A **transition metal** is a d-block element that **forms at least one ion with a partially filled d sub-shell**. Scandium ($\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}$, $3d^0$) and zinc ($\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$, $3d^{10}$) are d-block elements but are not transition metals.

**(ii)** First (3d) series, in order of atomic number 21 to 30:

$\mathrm{Sc}, \mathrm{Ti}, \mathrm{V}, \mathrm{Cr}, \mathrm{Mn}, \mathrm{Fe}, \mathrm{Co}, \mathrm{Ni}, \mathrm{Cu}, \mathrm{Zn}$

(Strictly only Ti to Cu are transition metals.)

**(iii)** Transition elements can show **variable oxidation states**, because the 3d and 4s electrons have similar energies; they can therefore form unstable intermediates by gaining and losing electrons easily. They also provide **vacant or partly filled d orbitals** on which reactant molecules can be adsorbed and weakened (heterogeneous catalysis). Examples: iron in the Haber process, vanadium(V) oxide in the contact process.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Consider the following complex compound $[\mathrm{Na_4Fe(CN)_6}]$

(i) Give the name of the complex the compound above.

(ii) State

A) the coordination number of iron in the complex compound

B) the oxidation state of iron in the complex compound

(iii) Draw the structure of the complex ion in b (i) and give its shape. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The complex ion is $[\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6}]^{4-}$, named the **hexacyanoferrate(II) ion**. The compound $\mathrm{Na_4[Fe(CN)_6]}$ is **sodium hexacyanoferrate(II)**.

**(ii)**

A) **Coordination number $= 6$**: six cyanide ligands are bonded to the iron(II) ion by dative covalent bonds, each through the carbon atom (lone pair on C).

B) **Oxidation state of iron $= +2$**: the complex ion has charge $4-$ (the four $\mathrm{Na^+}$ balance it), and six $\mathrm{CN^-}$ contribute $6 \times (-1) = -6$, so $x + (-6) = -4$ and $x = +2$.

**(iii)** The complex ion is **octahedral** (6 ligands, no lone pair on iron, bond angle $90^\circ$ between neighbouring ligands). Fe is at the centre; the six $\mathrm{CN^-}$ ligands lie along the $+x$, $-x$, $+y$, $-y$, $+z$, $-z$ axes, bonded to Fe through carbon ($\mathrm{Fe{-}C{\equiv}N}$):

```
              NC
              |   CN
              |  /
       NC ---Fe--- CN
            / |
          CN  |
              CN
        [Fe(CN)6]4-  octahedral
```

(Plain line: in the plane of the paper; the two ligands drawn obliquely are one behind and one in front of the plane.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Give the formula of a fertilizer containing nitrogen and sulphur atoms and state the oxidation state of nitrogen and sulphur in the compound.

| Formula of fertilizer | Oxidation state of Nitrogen | Oxidation state of sulphur |
|---|---|---|
| | | |

*[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Fertilizer: **ammonium sulphate**, $(\mathrm{NH_4})_2\mathrm{SO_4}$.

- Nitrogen, in $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$: $x + 4(+1) = +1$, so the oxidation state of N is $-3$.
- Sulphur, in $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$: $x + 4(-2) = -2$, so the oxidation state of S is $+6$.

| Formula of fertilizer | Oxidation state of Nitrogen | Oxidation state of sulphur |
|---|---|---|
| $(\mathrm{NH_4})_2\mathrm{SO_4}$ | $-3$ | $+6$ |

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) (i) Give two differences in chemical property between carbon or its compounds and the rest of the group IV elements. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Catenation and "the inert pair effect" are two phenomena that characterize the chemistry of the Group IV elements. What do you understand by;

A. Catenation?

B. Inert pair effect?

(iii) Explain why carbon shows a very high ability to catenate? *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Two differences** (any two):

1. **Hydrolysis of the tetrachlorides.** $\mathrm{CCl_4}$ is not hydrolysed by water, whereas $\mathrm{SiCl_4}$, $\mathrm{GeCl_4}$ and $\mathrm{SnCl_4}$ are hydrolysed rapidly: $\mathrm{SiCl_4} + 4\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{Si(OH)_4} + 4\mathrm{HCl}$. Carbon has no vacant d orbitals (only the $2s$ and $2p$ orbitals) and cannot expand its octet, so it cannot accept a lone pair from water; the other elements can use vacant d orbitals. For the same reason carbon has a maximum covalency of 4, but silicon forms $\mathrm{SiF_6^{2-}}$.
2. **Multiple bonds and oxides.** Carbon forms stable double and triple bonds ($\mathrm{C{=}C}$, $\mathrm{C{\equiv}C}$, $\mathrm{C{=}O}$) by $p\pi{-}p\pi$ overlap; the other elements do not, so $\mathrm{CO_2}$ is a gas made of small molecules $\mathrm{O{=}C{=}O}$ while $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ is a giant covalent solid.

**(ii)**

A. **Catenation** is the **ability of atoms of an element to bond to one another to form long chains and rings** (as in alkanes, polymers, graphite layers).

B. The **inert pair effect** is the **reluctance of the two outer $ns^2$ electrons to take part in bonding** in the heavier elements of the group. Down the group the oxidation state $+2$ becomes more stable and $+4$ less stable: $\mathrm{Ge}$ and $\mathrm{Sn}$ are mostly $+4$ with $\mathrm{Sn^{2+}}$ reducing, but for lead $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ is more stable than $\mathrm{Pb^{4+}}$, and $\mathrm{PbO_2}$ is a strong oxidising agent.

**(iii) Why carbon catenates so well.** Carbon atoms are **small**, so the $\mathrm{C{-}C}$ bond is **short and very strong** (about $348\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, compared with about $222\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ for $\mathrm{Si{-}Si}$). The chains are also **kinetically stable**: the $\mathrm{C{-}C}$ and $\mathrm{C{-}H}$ bonds are not attacked by water or oxygen at room temperature because carbon has no vacant d orbitals to accept a lone pair, whereas $\mathrm{Si{-}Si}$ bonds are easily broken. Carbon forms four covalent bonds and so can make branched chains, rings and multiple bonds.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(e) The group IV elements also exhibit allotropy.

(i) What is allotropy?

(ii) Give two crystalline forms of each of the following group IV elements:

Carbon

Tin *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Allotropy** is the **existence of an element in two or more different forms in the same physical state**, the forms differing in the arrangement of the atoms (and so in physical properties), for example the different crystal structures of one solid element.

**(ii) Crystalline forms.**

- **Carbon:** **diamond** (each C bonded tetrahedrally to four others, giant covalent lattice, very hard, non-conductor) and **graphite** (layers of hexagons, each C bonded to three others, soft, conducts electricity). A third crystalline form is the fullerenes (for example $\mathrm{C_{60}}$).
- **Tin:** **grey tin** ($\alpha$-tin, diamond-type cubic structure, stable below about $13\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$) and **white tin** ($\beta$-tin, tetragonal, metallic, stable above about $13\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$). A third form, rhombic tin, exists above about $161\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
